routes.description: Establish Christianity through a cumulative metaphysical route from unavoidable logic and contingent reality to a necessary self-relating Logos, then identify its universal, particular, and individual structure with the Trinity and defend the coherence of divine self-knowledge, creation, and hiddenness.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if indispensable logical and explanatory relations require a necessary mental ground, the proposed structure warrants a specifically Trinitarian identification rather than generic theism, and the account remains coherent under objections concerning divine perfection, revelation, creation, and hiddenness.

motionBridge.description: Connect the necessary self-relating Logos to distinctively Christian Trinitarian truth rather than stopping at logic, a first cause, idealism, or generic divinity.

centralBridges.description: Show that logic is unavoidable and describes the objective self-relating structure of reality requiring the proposed Logos account.
Show that contingent reality and rational explanation terminate in an uncaused necessary foundation rather than an infinite regress or brute physical fact.
Justify identifying the interdependence of universality, particularity, and individuality with a mental and specifically Trinitarian Logos.
Reconcile divine perfection and timeless knowledge with self-relation, doubt, creation, and contingent truths without introducing contradiction or dependence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how natural reason can disclose the relevant Trinitarian structure while accounting for Christianity's historical and incarnational claims.
Show why religious doubt, historical variation, divine transcendence, and creation from nothing remain compatible with the proposed God.

routes.description: Reject the motion by applying correspondence, demonstration, and explanatory economy to the Logos case, showing that its inferences do not establish a unique necessary mind or Christianity and that hiddenness and internal tensions provide contrary evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if logic and reality can be treated without adding God, the transitions from first cause or logical categories to a mind and Trinity remain unsupported, or the proposed Christian account conflicts with divine perfection, historical accessibility, classical logic, or expected evidence.

motionBridge.description: Connect the affirmative case's evidential, inferential, or coherence failures to withholding affirmation that Christianity is true and to any supported contrary inference.

centralBridges.description: Defend correspondence with demonstrable reality and minimal explanatory commitments as the appropriate standard for the Christian truth claim.
Show that a regress terminus, necessary foundation, logical structure, or mind does not establish a unique cause, Trinity, incarnation, or Catholic Christianity.
Show that an omniscient perfect mind cannot genuinely doubt, learn, deliberate, or correct itself in the manner required by the affirmative account.
Defend content-neutral classical logical laws against the dialectical unity of opposites used to support the affirmative metaphysics.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why divine hiddenness, unanswered prayer, religious competition, and historical variation count against the expected Christian world.
Distinguish conclusions arguably available through natural reason from historical claims about Jesus that require otherwise unavailable testimony or revelation.

sections.title: Truth Standards, Evidence, and Divine Hiddenness
sections.rationale: The motion requires a standard for affirming religious truth and an account of whether divine silence, disagreement, prayer, and historical variation fit or undermine Christianity.

sections.title: Grounding Logic and the Logos
sections.rationale: The central affirmative framework treats logic as unavoidable and as reality's objective self-relating structure, while the skeptical alternative disputes that God adds necessary grounding or explanation.

sections.title: Necessary Cause, Contingency, and Explanatory Termination
sections.rationale: The route from contingent reality to an uncaused foundation must establish an adequate terminus and address whether uniqueness, mentality, and explanatory resources follow from causal termination.

sections.title: From Metaphysical Structure to Trinity, Incarnation, and Revelation
sections.rationale: Christianity requires bridging generic metaphysical conclusions to the Trinity and historically specific claims about Jesus while resolving what natural reason can establish without revelation or testimony.

sections.title: Perfect Divine Knowledge, Doubt, and Self-Relation
sections.rationale: The extended dispute over whether perfect knowledge can include falsification, doubt, recursive correction, or foreknown resolution directly tests the coherence of the proposed Trinitarian mind and incarnation.

sections.title: Creation, Divine Relations, Spacetime, and Logical Coherence
sections.rationale: Claims about timeless creation, contingent truths, transcendence, spacetime, and unity of opposites test whether the proposed God can relate to creation without dependence, change, or conflict with classical logic.

moves.speaker: Lewis Howitt (PerspectivePhilosophy)
moves.proposition: Christianity has an epistemological advantage because the indispensable laws underlying rational inference ultimately point toward God.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Lewis the floor, and the uninterrupted opening statement remains his through this source window.

response.rationale: Constructive opening move proposing that rational inference needs an ultimate ground and that this provides Christianity an epistemological advantage.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly introduces the grounding thesis, though its decisive bridge from indispensable logic to God remains compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The grounding claim is recoverable, but the senses of grounding and epistemological advantage are not fully distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move presents an advantage for Christianity before supplying the bridge from logical indispensability to a divine ground.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The proposal is intelligible, but the indispensable-logic-to-God inference remains a material unstated bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt principally defines grounding and announces the thesis without representative support or rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central logic-ground bridge, although it does not yet complete that bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive span does not meaningfully engage a developed competing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stresses Christianity's epistemological advantage and defines grounding as locating the rational root of inference.

moves.speaker: Lewis Howitt (PerspectivePhilosophy)
moves.proposition: Contingent reality and rational inference require an uncaused necessary first cause, while an infinite causal regress would undermine reason itself.
moves.attributionBasis: This is a continuous portion of Lewis's timed opening statement with no intervening speaker transition.

response.rationale: Constructive move argues from contingent causal chains and rational inference to an uncaused necessary first cause.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely develops the necessary-foundation route but compresses the rejection of regress and alternative termini.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion and causal terminology are clear, but the universal scope over contingent beings is insufficiently qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Necessity is asserted although the excerpt does not establish that regress undermines inference or that only one terminus is possible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument has a usable structure, but it conflates necessary inferential relations with a necessary causal terminus.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central anti-regress and causal-to-rational warrants are asserted rather than defended against serious alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly addresses the indispensable necessary-foundation bridge and states its intended completion condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: No sufficiently developed rival account is examined within this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says all contingent beings lead to a necessary first cause and connects that conclusion to rational inference.

moves.speaker: Lewis Howitt (PerspectivePhilosophy)
moves.proposition: A brute physical first cause is insufficient because rational explanation requires a necessary relation from origin to end and a self-actualizing logical foundation.
moves.attributionBasis: The remarks continue Lewis's opening in his first-person argumentative voice until he identifies the proposed foundation with the Christian God.

response.rationale: Constructive move rejects a brute physical origin because it allegedly cannot explain inference, telos, or self-actualizing logic.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It materially supports the necessary-foundation route, but its added telos requirement is introduced without adequate derivation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is recoverable, though last cause, telos, and logical foundation shift between explanatory roles.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical inadequacy of brute foundations is stronger than the supplied argument establishing a required final cause.

charity.alternative: A brute physical terminus could ground causal existence without grounding norms of inference.
charity.decisiveQualification: That alternative separates causal explanation from logical or teleological explanation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference depends on an unsupported transition from first-cause explanation to a required telos and logical agency.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The physical alternatives are named, but their alleged inability to support rational argument is largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the necessary-foundation bridge by challenging a major brute-physical rival.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mentions the brute-fact alternative but dismisses it without answering the decisive separation of explanatory tasks.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names a quantum field, universe, and brute fact, then claims a first cause also needs a telos.

moves.speaker: Lewis Howitt (PerspectivePhilosophy)
moves.proposition: The mutually related logical moments of universality, particularity, and individuality constitute the divine Trinity and ground rational argumentation.
moves.attributionBasis: Lewis explicitly develops the three logical moments during the concluding portion of his uninterrupted opening statement.

response.rationale: Constructive move identifies combined logical moments with the Christian Trinity and makes that unity the basis of rational argument.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attempts the motion-level Christian identification, though the correspondence between categories and persons is compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The Trinitarian identification is clear, but logical moments, divine persons, and their unity are insufficiently differentiated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that an absolute self-understanding being can only contain these moments and be Trinitarian outruns the stated warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The categories-to-Trinity transition is a central non sequitur unless a substantive identity or entailment bridge is supplied.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Appeal to Aquinas and Christian naming does not independently establish that the logical structure is the Trinity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly attempts the motion bridge from metaphysical logic to distinctively Christian Trinitarian truth.

representationalCharity.rationale: The span advances its own identification without presenting a developed alternative mapping.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says absolute self-understanding contains all logical moments and that Christianity knows this unity as the Trinity.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Truth should be assessed by correspondence with demonstrable reality rather than grounded in God's mind or affirmed without sufficient evidence.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the opening to Matt, whose uninterrupted first-person remarks and explicit contrast with Lewis fill the window.

components.text: Whether Christianity gains an epistemological advantage by grounding inference in God.
Whether naming the logical ground as the Christian God establishes correspondence with reality.

response.rationale: The correspondence standard directly contests the claimed epistemological advantage, but it does not specifically analyze the Trinitarian mapping.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive epistemic demand but only partially answers the affirmative's metaphysical grounding argument.

precisionFindings.rationale: Correspondence, model inclusion, and insufficient evidence are clearly distinguished and conditionally framed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker limits the conclusion to not having seen sufficient evidence and allows God into the model if demonstrated.

charity.alternative: God's mind could be the metaphysical ground of truth rather than a competing empirical object.
charity.decisiveQualification: That metaphysical proposal still needs a demonstrated connection to the reality with which claims correspond.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional model and evidential standard are consistent, with only a bounded gap about why correspondence is exhaustive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The standard is clearly defended in conceptual terms, though no detailed evidence comparison is provided here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central truth-standard bridge without itself making the full motion-level defeat.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly permits a God-consistent model while insisting that the grounding proposal requires evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines truth as correspondence with reality, permits God if evidenced, and states that sufficient evidence has not been seen.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Divine hiddenness, denominational conflict, unanswered prayer, and persistent religious disagreement make the observed world unlike what Christianity leads us to expect if its God exists.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt continues his uninterrupted opening, moving from falsifiability to the hiding-person analogy and then explicitly to divine hiddenness.

components.text: Whether indispensable inference provides an epistemological advantage for Christianity.
Whether the proposed Trinity predicts the observed pattern of religious access and disagreement.

response.rationale: Hiddenness supplies issue-bearing contrary evidence about Christianity, but it does not answer either earlier grounding inference in the selected span.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer to the available earlier affirmative moves, despite materially advancing a separate skeptical burden.

precisionFindings.rationale: The expectation-based hiddenness claim is recoverable, with a bounded implicit dependence on the kind of God Christianity predicts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The probabilistic claim is appropriately framed, though the expected degree of disclosure is not expressly defended.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The expectation mismatch is coherent but leaves the relevant divine intentions and expected evidence as a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several observed phenomena are invoked, but their frequency and likelihood under competing hypotheses are not developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary hiddenness-disagreement bridge and reaches its upper tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt does not engage a developed affirmative explanation of hiddenness.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls hiddenness a strong argument and says the world differs from what would be expected if God existed.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Arguments for a first cause or logical ground do not establish the distinctive attributes, doctrines, practices, or historical claims of Christianity or Catholicism.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening remains Matt's, and he explicitly contrasts abstract grounding arguments with specific Christian and Catholic commitments.

components.text: Whether logical grounding establishes Christianity's distinctive Trinitarian and historical claims.
Whether an uncaused first cause is enough to identify Christianity.

response.rationale: The response diagnoses that generic grounding and first-cause conclusions lack the additional evidence needed for Christian and Catholic specificity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the missing inferential steps and states why the earlier conclusions cannot complete the Christian route.

charity.decisiveQualification: It must still supply an identity bridge and evidence for historical or denominational particulars.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well supported, though the excerpt does not inventory every alleged doctrinal step.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the motion-level condition for withholding affirmation of Christianity from generic premises.

representationalCharity.rationale: The critique allows an interesting line of reasoning while accurately retaining the decisive specificity requirement.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says doctrines and Catholic commitments are far removed from logic grounding and require their own evidence.

moves.speaker: Lewis Howitt (PerspectivePhilosophy)
moves.proposition: Logic is the objective structure of reality, and its mutually dependent universal, particular, and individual moments are intelligible as the Christian Logos and Trinity.
moves.attributionBasis: After Matt's challenge, Lewis resumes in first person and gives a sustained account of logical realism and Trinitarian metaphysics through the end of the response.

components.text: Whether the Logos account is merely prior idealist assumption rather than an explanation of objective reality.
Whether objective logical structure uniquely warrants the Christian Logos and Trinity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts both demands, but the decisive uniqueness and evidential bridges remain asserted rather than resolved.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim that the structure is only intelligible as the Christian God is substantially stronger than the supplied explanation.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Identifying God with logic does not justify treating the logical categories of universality, particularity, and unity as the persons of the Trinity.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained first-person critique and its direct recap of Lewis's preceding account clearly identify Matt as the speaker.

components.text: Whether universal, particular, and individual logical categories are literally the Trinitarian persons.
Whether the initial logical-moments argument justifies its Trinitarian mapping.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies the unsupported literal mapping and explains that assigning categories to persons does not establish identity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly targets the decisive inference and states the defeating consequence for both formulations of the mapping.

precisionFindings.rationale: The difference between metaphorical comparison and literal identification is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker frames the criticism as how the account appears and avoids claiming a formal contradiction.

charity.alternative: The categories may be proposed as an ontological identity rather than a decorative metaphor.
charity.decisiveQualification: An ontological identity still requires an argument beyond assigning each category a Christian name.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central trinitarian-identification bridge at the top of the central tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response recognizes the intended literal claim and criticizes its absent justification rather than reducing it to metaphor.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt recapitulates the category-to-person assignments and challenges their presentation as an actual rather than metaphorical mapping.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even if a causal regress terminates in something noncontingent, neither a unique terminus nor its containing every later possibility has been established.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage answers Lewis's first-cause questions in Matt's characteristic skeptical first-person voice and develops his match-and-fuel counterexample.

components.text: Whether causal termination establishes one necessary first cause containing all later possibilities.
Whether a terminus must contain the rational and teleological resources attributed to it.

response.rationale: The reply grants a possible noncontingent terminus while diagnosing that uniqueness and comprehensive potential do not follow.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly attacks the decisive inferential overreach and supplies a counterexample structure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The concessions about termination are separated clearly from doubts about uniqueness and contained potential.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Repeated uncertainty language appropriately limits the claim to underdetermination rather than proving a rival ontology.

charity.alternative: A first cause might need sufficient causal resources for every downstream effect.
charity.decisiveQualification: Causal sufficiency does not by itself establish one entity or literal containment of every possibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between termination, uniqueness, and modal containment is coherent and defeats the compressed inference.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the necessary-foundation bridge by showing that the proposed terminus is underdetermined.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response grants termination and necessity while isolating the stronger conclusions that remain unsupported.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes a possible noncontingent first thing but denies that it must be unique or contain every later potential.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Establishing that a necessary logos is a mind would still leave many unsupported steps before identifying it with the specifically Catholic Trinity.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker directly answers Lewis's proposed next step and contrasts a generic mind with the Catholic Trinity in Matt's skeptical framing.

components.text: Whether establishing a necessary mental Logos identifies the specifically Catholic Trinity.
Whether logical moments close the distance from a mind to the Trinity.

response.rationale: The reply expressly grants the proposed mind as a first step and identifies the many unargued steps to Catholic Trinitarian specificity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive specificity demand, though the hyperbolic step count substitutes for a detailed inventory.

precisionFindings.rationale: The generic-mind and Catholic-Trinity endpoints are clear; the numerical exaggeration is expressly disclaimed.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited conclusion that further steps are required is fully warranted and explicitly qualified against literal exaggeration.

charity.alternative: The affirmative may offer logical moments as intermediate steps from mind to Trinity.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those intermediate identifications still require independent justification and do not yield Catholic specificity automatically.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The gap objection is valid and consistent, with only rhetorical compression in place of enumerated missing premises.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The logical burden is accurately identified, though the excerpt gives limited detail about the specific missing doctrines.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central generic-to-specific gap by distinguishing a necessary mind from Catholic Trinity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response acknowledges the mind as a genuine first step while preserving the decisive unsupported distance.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants showing a mind as a first step and emphasizes numerous further steps to the Catholic Trinity.

moves.speaker: Lewis Howitt (PerspectivePhilosophy)
moves.proposition: The spiritual truths of the Trinity are accessible through natural reason and observation without dependence on scriptural revelation or knowledge of Christianity's historical narrative.
moves.attributionBasis: Lewis invokes Aquinas, describes his own near-perennialist view, and expressly distinguishes natural reasoning from reliance on scripture.

components.text: Whether the Trinitarian structure requires scripture or can be reached through natural reason.
Whether natural reason establishes Christianity's historical and denominational particulars.
Whether natural observation justifies the specific logical mapping to Trinitarian persons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It answers a secondary access component while failing to resolve the decisive identity and historical-specificity demands.

precisionFindings.rationale: The natural-reason thesis is clear, but spiritual truths and Trinity are not specified enough to fix the conclusion's scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The personal and qualified framing is cautious, yet accessibility is asserted without demonstrating the natural inference.

charity.alternative: Historical incarnation claims may require testimony even if abstract triadic metaphysics is naturally accessible.
charity.decisiveQualification: Access to a triadic structure does not itself disclose Jesus, incarnation, or Catholic historical claims.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Natural access is compatible with the framework, but the inference from observation to Trinitarian spiritual truth remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Aquinas and personal method are invoked, but the promised natural inference is not demonstrated in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary reason-access bridge at the top of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response expressly sets history aside, thereby leaving the strongest specificity qualification unresolved.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Natural reasoning cannot disclose the historical and incarnational claim that Jesus was divine and human to beings with no knowledge of humanity or earthly events.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt develops the alien hypothetical through a sequence of questions about Jesus, humanity, and what Klingons could discover before encountering humans.

components.text: Whether natural reason alone can disclose the incarnational claim that Jesus is divine and human.
Whether abstract logical particularity identifies the historical person Jesus.

response.rationale: The alien hypothetical diagnoses that abstract reason lacks the historical and human information required for incarnation claims.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive access demand and states why the historical identification cannot follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hypothetical cleanly distinguishes abstract divine particularity from knowledge of humanity and Jesus.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The informational limitation follows from the stipulated absence of human and earthly knowledge.

charity.alternative: Natural reason might disclose that God can have concrete particular existence without naming Jesus.
charity.decisiveQualification: That generic modal conclusion remains insufficient for the historical divine-human identity claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The information-gap argument clearly distinguishes what the hypothetical reasoners could infer from what history supplies.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment specifically supports the epistemic limitation, with a bounded gap about all possible natural theology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary reason-revelation gap and nearly exhausts that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response allows abstract particularity while accurately preserving the decisive historical access gap.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how beings ignorant of humans could infer that Jesus was both God and human through reason alone.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: A perfect mind cannot be imperfect, should know that it is perfect, and therefore could have no reason to doubt its own perfection.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Matt the floor, after which Matt states the argument as a compact conditional sequence and ends by naming its question.

components.text: Whether the proposed divine self-relation is coherent with a perfect mind's self-knowledge.
Whether a perfect Logos could include genuine doubt as a logical moment.

response.rationale: The compact conditional directly challenges the coherence of divine doubt given perfection and perfect self-knowledge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the relevant divine-coherence implication, although the earlier moves only indirectly develop doubt.

precisionFindings.rationale: Perfect mind, self-knowledge, imperfection, and doubt are used consistently in the compact conditional.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stated conception of perfection, the incompatibility with uncertainty about perfection is proportionately asserted.

charity.alternative: Doubt might be a represented possibility rather than an actually entertained uncertainty in God.
charity.decisiveQualification: The objection succeeds only against genuine doubt or epistemic uncertainty, not mere awareness of alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional is valid under its stable conception of perfect self-knowledge, with one bounded ambiguity about doubt.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual premises are explicit and mutually supporting, though the intended type of divine doubt needs clarification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central perfect-mind objection and isolates its decisive coherence test.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument is fair but leaves this bounded distinction between genuine doubt and represented falsifiability implicit.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that a perfect mind cannot be imperfect, must know its perfection, and thus cannot doubt it.

moves.proposition: Divine doubt need not obtain as an imperfection; it can be a moment of falsifiable self-knowledge that is overcome and unified within the Trinitarian process.

components.text: Whether any moment of doubt is incompatible with God's perfect self-knowledge.

moves.attributionBasis: The passage defines a perfect mind as a thinking thing incapable of error and consistently develops Matt's no-process account of perfect knowledge.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Presupposing God is unnecessary because logic and the universe suffice pragmatically, while invoking God merely relocates rather than resolves the unexplained foundation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Matt, and the sustained skeptical answer uses his characteristic first-person framing without a speaker change.

components.text: Whether invoking God explains the inviolability and objective authority of logic.
Whether a divine ground adds explanatory value beyond using logic and observing the universe.

response.rationale: The response diagnoses explanatory relocation: positing God to guarantee logic leaves the foundation unexplained rather than adding a demonstrated mechanism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts the grounding demand and states the defeating explanatory consequence, despite some rhetorical excess.

precisionFindings.rationale: Pragmatic use, explanation, presupposition, and divine guarantee are distinguishable throughout the critique.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The admitted lack of a full explanation is well calibrated, though calling the divine proposal invented is rhetorically stronger than shown.

charity.alternative: God could explain logic by being its necessary ontological ground rather than an additional unexplained object.
charity.decisiveQualification: That alternative needs independent explanatory content showing why divine necessity clarifies logical necessity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory-regress objection is coherent, with a bounded gap about whether all ultimate explanations require further explanation.

moves.proposition: God can be present within spacetime while exceeding it because spacetime is internally contained within God rather than limiting God.

components.text: Whether God's relation to created spacetime gives God contingent relational properties.

components.text: Whether presence in multiple places or transcendence violates excluded middle.
